en: Thus have I heard: the Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta, the thirty-first discourse in the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Nādika in the Brick House.
Now at that time the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimbila were dwelling in the Gosiṅga Sāla-tree Grove.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the Gosiṅga Sāla-tree Grove.
The park keeper saw the Blessed One coming from afar.
Having seen him, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Do not enter this park, ascetic."
"Three sons of good family dwell here who are intent on their own welfare;
do not cause them any discomfort.
The Venerable Anuruddha overheard the park keeper conversing with the Blessed One.
Having heard this, he said to the park keeper:
"Friend park keeper, do not stop the Blessed One.
Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived."
Then the Venerable Anuruddha approached the Venerable Nandiya and the Venerable Kimila; having approached them, he said to the Venerable Nandiya and the Venerable Kimila:
"Come forth, venerable sirs, come forth! The Blessed One, our Teacher, has arrived.
Then the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila went out to meet the Blessed One.
One received the Blessed One’s bowl and robe; one prepared a seat; one set out water for washing the feet.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One washed his feet.
Having approached the Blessed One, those venerable ones paid homage to him and sat down to one side.
As the venerable Anuruddha was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"I hope it is bearable for you, Anuruddhas; I hope you are getting by; I hope you are not suffering from lack of almsfood?"
“It is bearable, Blessed One; it is sustainable, Blessed One; and we are not distressed by lack of almsfood, Bhante.
“But, Anuruddhas, do you dwell in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, like milk and water, regarding one another with eyes of love?
“Indeed, Bhante, we dwell in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, like milk and water, regarding one another with eyes of love.”
“But in what way, Anuruddhas, do you dwell in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, like milk and water mixed together, looking upon one another with eyes of love?
“Here, venerable sir, this thought occurs to me:
‘It is a gain for me, truly it is a great gain for me!’”
‘I am living together with fellow practitioners of the holy life who are such as these.
Venerable sir, toward these venerable ones, I maintain a friendly bodily action both openly and in private;
I maintain a friendly verbal action both openly and in private.
“Benevolent mental action is established in me, both openly and in private.
Regarding this, venerable sir, it occurs to me:
‘What if I were to set aside my own mind and conduct myself according to the minds of these very venerable ones?’”
"Thus, venerable sir, having set aside my own mind, I conduct myself according to the minds of these very venerable ones.
For indeed, venerable sir, we have different bodies, yet it seems to me that we have a single mind.
Venerable Nandiya also [said the same]...pe...
The Venerable Kimila also said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it occurs to me as well:
‘It is indeed a gain for me, it is indeed a great fortune for me!’”
‘I am living together with fellow practitioners of the holy life who are such as these.
Venerable sir, toward these venerable ones, I maintain a friendly bodily action both openly and in private;
I maintain a friendly verbal action both openly and in private.
“Bhante, I maintain an attitude of loving-kindness through mental action, both openly and in private.
It occurs to me, Bhante:
‘What if I were to set aside my own mind and conduct myself according to the minds of these very venerable ones?’”
“Thus, venerable sir, having set aside my own mind, I conduct myself according to the mind of these very venerable ones.
For indeed, venerable sir, we have different bodies, yet it seems as if we have a single mind.
“In this way, venerable sir, we dwell in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, like milk and water mixed together, looking upon one another with eyes of love.”
“Excellent, excellent, Anuruddhas!
But I hope, Anuruddhas, that you dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute?
“Indeed, Bhante, we dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute.”
“But in what way, Anuruddhas, do you dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute?
“Here, venerable sir, whichever of us first returns from the village with almsfood prepares the seats, sets out water for drinking and water for washing, and puts out a refuse bucket.

Whoever returns last from the village with almsfood, if there is food left over and he wishes to eat, he does so; if he does not wish to eat, he throws it away where there is no greenery or drops it into water where there are no living beings.”
Thus he puts away the seats, puts away the drinking water and the washing water, puts away the refuse bowl, and sweeps the dining hall.
Whoever sees that the water-jug for drinking, the water-jug for washing, or the toilet-jug is empty or depleted, refills it.

If there is something too heavy for him to lift, he calls a second person by a gesture of the hand and fills it by passing it from hand to hand; yet, venerable sir, we do not break out into speech on that account.
“Moreover, Bhante, every five days we sit together for an entire night in talk on the Dhamma.
It is in this way, Bhante, that we dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute.
“Excellent, excellent, Anuruddhas! Excellent, excellent!”
“But, Anuruddhas, as you dwell thus diligent, ardent, and resolute, have you attained any superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a dwelling in comfort?
“Why not, Bhante?

Here, Bhante, as much as we wish, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, we enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.”

“Venerable sir, while we were dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, we have attained this further distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a superior state beyond human condition, a comfortable abiding.
“Excellent, excellent, Anuruddhas!

But, Anuruddhas, for the transcending of this abiding and for the subsiding of this abiding, has there been attained another distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a superior state beyond human condition, a comfortable abiding?”
“What could it be for us, Bhante? Here, Bhante, as soon as we wish, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought,

we enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and is born of concentration, filled with rapture and happiness.

“Venerable sir, by transcending this dwelling and by the subsiding of this dwelling, we have attained another superior state of easeful living, a distinction of noble knowledge and vision beyond human reach.
“Excellent, excellent, Anuruddhas!

But, Anuruddhas, by transcending this dwelling and by the subsiding of this dwelling, has there been attained another superior state of easeful living, a distinction of noble knowledge and vision beyond human reach?”
“What could it be for us, Bhante?

Here, Bhante, as much as we wish, with the fading away of rapture, we dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body—of which the Noble Ones declare: ‘He who is equanimous…”
‘mindful and dwelling in happiness,’ we entered and dwelt in the third jhāna.
By transcending this dwelling and by the subsiding of this dwelling, another distinction of noble knowledge and vision, surpassing human states, a state of ease, has been attained.
“Excellent, excellent, Anuruddhas!

“But, Anuruddhas, by transcending this dwelling and by allaying this dwelling, has another superior state—a distinction of noble knowledge and vision beyond human condition, a comfortable abiding—been attained?
“How could it not be so, Bhante?
Here, Bhante, as much as we desire, through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, even before...”
"With the subsiding of both joy and dejection, we enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
By transcending this dwelling, and by the stilling of this dwelling, another distinction of noble knowledge and vision, surpassing human states, has been attained— a comfortable abiding."
“Excellent, excellent, Anuruddhas!

But, Anuruddhas, by transcending this dwelling and by bringing this dwelling to rest, has another superior attainment—a distinction of knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a state of ease beyond human condition—been reached?
“How could that not be so, Bhante?”

“Here, venerable sir, as soon as we wish, by completely surmounting perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] ‘space is infinite,’ we enter and dwell in the base of infinite space.
By the surmounting of this dwelling and the subsiding of this dwelling, another distinction of knowledge and vision higher than the human state has been attained: a comfortable dwelling.”
“Excellent, excellent, Anuruddhas!

But, Anuruddhas, by transcending this dwelling and by bringing this dwelling to rest, has another superior state—a distinction of knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding—been attained?
“How could that not be so, Bhante?”
"Here, venerable sir, as far as we wish, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, perceiving ‘infinite consciousness,’ we enter and dwell in the base of infinite consciousness...
Having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving ‘there is nothing,’ we enter and dwell in the base of nothingness...
Having completely transcended the base of nothingness, we enter and dwell in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."

“Venerable sir, by transcending this dwelling and by the subsiding of this dwelling, we have attained another superior state of easeful living, a distinction of noble knowledge and vision beyond human conditions.
“Excellent, excellent, Anuruddhas!

But, Anuruddhas, by transcending that dwelling and by the subsiding of that dwelling, has there been attained another superior state of easeful living, a distinction of noble knowledge and vision beyond human conditions?”
“What could we not have, Bhante?

Here, Bhante, as much as we desire, having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, we enter and dwell in the cessation of perception and feeling; and by seeing with wisdom, our taints are utterly destroyed.
By transcending this dwelling and by the subsiding of this dwelling, another distinction of noble knowledge and vision, surpassing human states, has been attained—a comfortable abiding.”
“Venerable sir, we do not see any other comfortable dwelling that is more excellent or more sublime than this comfortable dwelling.
“Excellent, excellent, Anuruddhas!
There is no comfortable dwelling more excellent or more sublime than this comfortable dwelling.”

Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat and departed.
Then the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila, having followed the Blessed One for a short distance and then turning back, said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:
“Did we perhaps inform the Venerable Anuruddha, saying:
‘We are attainers of these and those meditative abidings and attainments,’ that the Venerable Anuruddha would proclaim before the Blessed One, up to the destruction of the taints?
“The Venerable ones did not inform me in such a way.”
‘We are attainers of these and those dwellings and meditative attainments’; moreover, by encompassing their minds with my own mind, I have known of the venerable ones:
‘These venerable ones are attainers of these and those dwellings and meditative attainments.
Deities, too, have informed me of this matter:
"These venerable ones are attainers of these various dwellings and meditative attainments.
When the Blessed One was thus questioned with this question, he replied.

Then the yakkha Dīgha Parajana approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the yakkha Dīgha Parajana said this to the Blessed One:
“It is indeed a gain for the Vajjis, a great gain for the Vajjian people,
that the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwells here, as do these three noble sons:
the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila.”
Having heard the cry of the long-lived yakkha, the earth-dwelling devas raised a shout: "It is a gain for the Vajjis,
it is a great gain for the Vajjian people,
that the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwells here, as do these three sons of noble family!"
“Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimila.
Having heard the cry of the earth-dwelling devas, the Cātumahārājika devas...
[and so on] ...the Tāvatiṃsa devas... [and so on].
The Yāma devas …pe… the Tusita devas …pe… the Nimmānarati devas …pe…
The Paranimmitavasavatti devas … [and so on] … down to the Brahmakāyika devas raised their voices, saying:
“It is indeed a gain for the Vajjis, a great gain for the Vajjian people!
"Wherever the Tathāgata dwells—the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One—and where these three sons of noble family dwell:
the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila.
Thus, at that very moment, at that very instant, at that very second, those venerable ones became known as far as the Brahma-world.
“It is so, Dīgha, it is so, Dīgha!

Because, Dīgha, these three sons of good family have gone forth from the home life into homelessness from that family—if that family were to recollect these three sons of good family with a confident mind, it would lead to that family’s welfare and happiness for a long time.
And because, Dīgha, these three sons of good family have gone forth from the home life into homelessness from that circle of families...”
If even an entire circle of kinsmen were to recollect these three sons of good family with a mind of confidence,
that circle of kinsmen would experience welfare and happiness for a long time. And,

Dīgha, if even the village from which these three sons of good family went forth from the home life into homelessness were to recollect these three sons of good family with a mind of confidence, that village would experience welfare and happiness for a long time.
Dīgha, if the town from which these three sons of good family went forth from the home life into homelessness were to recollect those three sons of good family with a confident mind,
that would lead to the welfare and happiness of that town for a long time.
Dīgha, if the city from which these three sons of good family went forth from the home life into homelessness were also [to do so]...
If those three sons of good family should be recollected with a confident heart by this city, it would lead to the welfare and happiness of that city for a long time.
And, Dīgha, as for that country from which these three sons of good family have gone forth from the home life into homelessness—
if that country should also recollect these three sons of good family with a confident heart, it would lead to the welfare and happiness of that country for a long time.
If all the kṣatriyas, Dīgha, were to recollect these three sons of good family with a confident mind, it would lead to the welfare and happiness of all those kṣatriyas for a long time.
If all the brahmins, Dīgha...
[and so on] ...if all the vaiśyas, Dīgha... [and so on].
If, Dīgha, all the *suddas* were to recollect these three sons of good family with a confident mind, it would lead to the welfare and happiness of all those *suddas* for a long time.
And if, Dīgha, the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans,
were to recollect these three sons of good family with a confident mind, it would lead to the welfare and happiness of that world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās...
"For the long-term welfare and happiness of this generation, including its brahmās, recluses, and brahmins, its devas and humans.

See, Dīgha, how far these three clansmen have set out for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of devas and humans.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Delighted, the long-lived non-human spirit (yakkha) rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
Thus ends the first discourse, the Cūḷagosiṅgasutta.
